description.en: As part of creation, humans are charged with the protection of trees. description.en: Water features prominently from the opening chapter of the Torah, as God separates between the waters of the sky and the waters below. Water plays a role in many other biblical narratives, like the splitting of the Red Sea or the miraculous supply of water provided to the people of Israel in the desert. Later Jewish sources discuss water extensively, acknowledging its physical necessity as a life-sustaining element and spiritual significance, and delving into details about its usage in Temple rituals, as a metaphor for Torah, and more.

In the opening chapter of the Torah, God creates the moon, alongside other celestial bodies, on the fourth day of creation. In Jewish tradition and practice, the moon plays a central role in determining the calendar: New Hebrew months start with the appearance of new moons, which also lead to the determination of holiday dates. Texts throughout the ages discuss the moon's symbolism and significance; halakhic practices related to the moon, like the concept of blessing the new moon; and ways in which the lunar calendar interacts with the solar calendar.

en.title: The Creation of Night and Day

en.prompt: The first chapter of Genesis describes how God created light and established the cycle of day and night.
en.ai_prompt: The creation of night and day by God marks the first day with the transition from evening to morning, highlighting the divine orchestration of time. The first chapter of Genesis describes how God created light and established the cycle of day and night, emphasizing the significance of both in the divine order.

description.en: Nighttime serves as the setting for pivotal moments in biblical history, including God’s [covenant of the pieces](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.15.12?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with Abraham, Jacob’s [wrestling](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.32.23?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with the angel, the [plague](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.12.29?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of the firstborn, and the [splitting of the sea](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.14.20?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic sources emphasize the special value of Torah study at night, teaching that a “[thread of kindness](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.12b.8?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)” accompanies those who engage in it, and many communities observe the custom of studying Torah throughout the night of Shavuot. Sources of Jewish thought and liturgy also portray the night as a particularly fitting time for introspection, devotion, prayer, and revelation.

en.title: The Beginning
en.prompt: Parashat Bereshit is the first portion of the Torah. It begins with an account of God’s creation of the world.

description.en: Bereshit ("In the Beginning”) is the first parashah in the annual Torah reading cycle, which restarts at the beginning of the book of Genesis. The reading begins with God’s creation of the world. The first people, Adam and Eve, eat from the Tree of Knowledge and are then banished from the Garden of Eden. Their elder son, Cain, kills their younger son, Abel, and Cain is destined to a life of wandering.

In the Bible, it is created on the fourth day of creation and features in key narratives such as Joseph's [dream](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.37.9?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) and the miracle of Joshua halting the sun, as well as in poetic [metaphors](https://www.sefaria.org/Judges.5.31?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic literature ties practices like daily prayer to sunrise and sunset and discusses the sun's role in structuring the calendar. Liturgical [texts](https://www.sefaria.org/Siddur_Sefard%2C_Shabbat_Morning_Services%2C_Shema_%26_Blessings.4?ven=hebrew|Torat_Emet_357&lang=bi) praise God for continually renewing creation and bringing forth the sun each day, and Jewish philosophical works develop the sun as a symbol of divine constancy.

Eating features from the outset of the Torah in the story of the garden of Eden, where Adam and Eve's [consumption](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.3.6?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of forbidden fruit shapes human history. Food serves as a central theme in many other biblical stories: Patriarchs and matriarchs [leave](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.12.10?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&sbsq=%D7%95%D7%99%D7%94%D7%99%20%D7%A8%D7%A2%D7%91%20%D7%91%D7%90%D7%A8%D7%A5&with=SidebarSearch&lang2=en) their homes during [famines](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.26.1?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&sbsq=%D7%95%D7%99%D7%94%D7%99%20%D7%A8%D7%A2%D7%91%20%D7%91%D7%90%D7%A8%D7%A5&with=SidebarSearch&lang2=en) in search of food to eat, Esau sells his birthright to eat a [bowl of soup](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.25.30?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&sbsq=%D7%94%D7%9C%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%98%D7%A0%D7%99&with=SidebarSearch&lang2=en), and the people of Israel repeatedly [complain](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.11.4?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) about food in the desert. Jewish texts explore many commandments and practices surrounding food, including feeding the hungry, reciting blessings before and after eating, observing the laws of kashrut, and eating certain foods during specific occasions (like matzah on Passover, for example).

Bereshit ("In the Beginning”) is the first parashah in the annual Torah reading cycle, which restarts at the beginning of the book of Genesis. The reading begins with God’s creation of the world. The first people, Adam and Eve, eat from the Tree of Knowledge and are then banished from the Garden of Eden. Their elder son, Cain, kills their younger son, Abel, and Cain is destined to a life of wandering.

description.en: Birds feature in the Jewish textual tradition from the opening chapter of the Torah, which [recounts](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.21?lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) how birds were created on the fifth day of creation. [Noah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/noah?tab=admin) uses birds to help determine whether it is safe to leave the ark, and other parts of the Torah discuss laws surrounding birds, like which ones are prohibited for consumption and the obligation to send away a mother bird before taking her young. Later Jewish texts expand on these concepts and other aspects of the nature and qualities of birds.

en.title: In the Image of God
en.prompt: The first chapter of Genesis describes how humankind was created in the divine image. For thousands of years, Jewish thinkers have pointed to this verse as a foundation of the idea that every individual is to be treated with dignity.
en.ai_prompt: Humankind was created in the divine image, which endows every individual with inherent dignity and equality. The first chapter of Genesis describes the creation of humankind by God, emphasizing that humans were made in the divine image and created as both male and female.

description.en: The opening chapter of the Torah describes how God created humanity [in the image of God](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.27?lang=he&with=all&lang2=en), a concept that fuels the idea that people are to be treated with dignity and respect. The value of human dignity stands behind many Jewish commandments and customs, such as the obligation to [return a cloak](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.24.13?lang=he&with=all&lang2=en) taken as collateral from a poor person as the night approaches, the duty to promptly [bury the dead](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.21.23?ven=english|The_Koren_Jerusalem_Bible&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en), and the commandment to respect the elderly. Rabbinic [sources](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.19b.2?lang=he&with=all&lang2=en) discuss situations in which human dignity can override other commandments, mystical texts explore the concept of developing one's inner spark, and ethical books expand upon ways to cultivate the trait of respect for others.

As part of creation, humans are charged with the protection of trees. Those trees that produce fruit in the land of Israel are subject to the various Torah regulations regarding Temple gifts and tithes. Trees are also likened to the Torah itself and serve as a popular metaphor in Jewish tradition.
description.he: בהיותם חלק מהבריאה, בני האדם מופקדים בהגנת ושמירת העצים. בתורה יש מצוות שונות החלות על עצי פרי בארץ ישראל כמו תרומות ומעשרות והבאת ביכורים למקדש. העץ הוא דימוי נפוץ במסורת היהודית לתורה עצמה וכן למי שמקיים אותה.

description.en: Time is a concept that appears from the very beginning of the Torah, as the world's creation unfolds over seven days, each of which is divided into evening and morning. Blessing is the act of calling down God's favor upon someone or something. The one calling down the blessing can be a person, an angel, or God Godself. Blessings are meant to bring benefits to their recipient, such as material goods or having many offspring. Tradition recognizes a four-part typology of liturgical blessings: on performing a commandment; in prayer; on partaking of sustenance; and in praise of God.

en.prompt: The earth's flora and fauna self-perpetuate naturally. The first chapter of the book of Genesis describes how God created the vegetation to bear its own seeds and fruit, to be fertile.
en.ai_context: God’s creation of the world includes creating biological species that self-perpetuate through reproduction.
en.ai_prompt: God's creation of vegetation that self-perpetuates through seed-bearing plants and fruit trees highlights the natural process of reproduction and the inherent fertility of the earth. The first chapter of Genesis describes how God created the world, including the vegetation that reproduces through seeds and fruit.

description.en: In Jewish texts and thought, it is God who grants fertility — whether agricultural bounty or children — through blessings and [rain](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/rain?tab=sources). Jewish texts and traditions include narratives of families struggling to conceive children, God opening wombs, prayers for rain, and more.

en.title: Mastery over Nature
en.prompt: When God finished creating humans, God blessed them. In the book of Genesis, the words God chooses for this blessing set up a specific power dynamic between humanity and the rest of creation.
en.ai_context: The book of Genesis declares human power over nature.

description.en: Power is often understood as a demonstrable, physical strength. However, an inner power of restraint is also seen as a sign of strength of character. The Jewish textual tradition frequently regards God as all-powerful, and this divine power is contrasted with the lesser power of mere mortals. The power expressed through ongoing creation, nature, and the world is presented in various genres as an emanation of God’s power.
